paper_metadata.title: Grain refinement during high temperature tensile testing of prior cold worked and peak aged Cu–Ti alloys: Evidence of superplasticity

evidence.quote: The high temperature tensile properties of solution treated, cold worked and peak aged Cu–1.5 wt.%Ti and Cu–4.5 wt.%Ti alloys have been investigated in the temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 550 ◦C.

parameters.cooling_method: cooled in vacuum in mould chamber

evidence.quote: A 30-kg melt each of Cu–Ti alloys with aimed Ti content of 1.5 and 4.5 wt.% was made in a graphite crucible of STOKES vacuum induction melting (VIM) furnace at a vacuum of 4 m and cast, after pouring at a temperature of 1230 ◦C into a graphite mould
The ingots were homogenised at 850 ◦C for 24 h and analysed for Ti content.
The ingots were subsequently hot forged and rolled after soaking at 850 ◦C for 2 h into wrought products (flats and rods) of suitable sizes.
The solution treatment was carried out by heating in a resistance heating furnace for 2 h at 750 ◦C for Cu–1.5Ti and 860◦C for Cu–4.5Ti alloy followed by rapid quenching in water.
Samples from the hot rolled flats were solution treated, cold rolled at room temperature to give 90% reduction in thickness and aged to attain peak strength.
The cold rolled strips were aged at 400 ◦C for 6 h and 1 h for Cu–1.5Ti and Cu–4.5Ti alloys, respectively, to attain maximum strength [7].

mechanisms.name: dislocation cutting of precipitates
mechanisms.material_state: peak aged, tested at up to 350 C

evidence.quote: Up to the test temperature of 350 ◦C, dislocations cut through the fine precipitate particles of β′.
Beyond 350 ◦C, both YS and TS decrease due to coarsening of the fine Cu4Ti, β′ precipitate particles.

mechanisms.name: thermally activated cross-slip
mechanisms.material_state: peak aged, tested at elevated temperature

evidence.quote: As the test temperature increased further, thermally activated cross-slip dominates which would make the movement of dislocations easy leading to continuous downfall of the strength.
Precipitation of equilibrium phase β, Cu3Ti, at the test temperature of 550 ◦C also contributes to the decrease in strength due to over aging
The increase in elongation is attributed to recovery and dynamic recrystallisation during testing at 450 ◦C as well as 550 ◦C.

mechanisms.name: grain growth restriction by second-phase particles

evidence.quote: They would have restricted the grain growth resulting in a very fine grain size of less than 1.0 m which has lead to superplasticity in Cu–4.5Ti alloy.
Therefore, it is concluded that cold worked (90%) and peak aged (at 400 ◦C) Cu–4.5Ti alloy exhibits superplastic behaviour when tensile tested at 550 ◦C at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1.
